passage:
"Siddharth, bhai, listen. My friend's group doubles your money in six weeks."
"Doubles? Who pays for the doubling, Sahil?"
"The trading guy. He's got screenshots. Proof."
"Screenshots aren't proof. Anyone can make those."
"You're so boring."
"Maybe. I'm putting a small amount every month into a regular fund. It's slow."
"Slow is useless."
"It's not flashy. But it's spread across lots of companies, so one bad one doesn't sink it."
"And if my guy is real?"
"If it's real, why is he in a chat group begging for your pocket money?"
"..."
"Just ask someone who knows before you send anything. Please."
"Fine. But if I miss out, I'm blaming you."

qa.q: How quickly did Sahil's friend's group claim to double money?
qa.a: They claimed to double it in six weeks.

qa.q: What does Sahil's 'You're so boring' suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He is excited by the idea of fast money and a bit irritated that Siddharth is questioning it.

qa.q: What would you advise Sahil to do next?
qa.a: Ask a trusted, knowledgeable adult or professional before sending any money, as Siddharth suggests.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see his own small monthly investment?
qa.a: He sees it as slow and unexciting but safer, because it is spread across many companies.

grounding: Shows a young person contrasting slow, spread-out investing with a get-rich-quick scheme.

passage: I'm Vishal, and when I got my first proper salary, I wanted to do something smart with it, so naturally I did something dumb. I put almost all my savings into one company's shares because a guy in my college group swore it would fly. It dropped by a third in a month. I didn't sleep well for days. My flatmate Irfan didn't mock me. He just showed me how he put a small, fixed sum every month into a fund that holds many companies, and how some months it went down, some up. 'I don't check it daily,' he said. That was the part I couldn't imagine. Now I do something similar, small and regular. It's less exciting. I sleep better.

qa.q: How much did Vishal's single share drop in a month?
qa.a: It dropped by a third in a month.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling after the shares fell, and how do you know?
qa.a: Vishal was anxious and regretful, and did not sleep well for days.

qa.q: Which approach worked better for Vishal, and why?
qa.a: Small, regular amounts in a fund holding many companies, because one bad company did not decide everything and the daily worry stopped.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt watching Vishal's mistake?
qa.a: He was probably sympathetic rather than smug, since he chose to show his own method instead of mocking.

grounding: Shows a young earner learning about spreading risk and steady small investing after chasing a hot tip.

passage:
Finance club note, Abhinav (faculty advisor), after Tuesday's session.

Disha, a second-year, stayed back after the talk on compounding. She had been quiet all hour, arms folded. She said her uncle had lost savings in a scheme promising fixed high returns, and she was now scared to invest anything at all. I did not push her toward any product. I asked what she already knew. She explained compounding back to me better than half the room could. We talked about how some risk is part of any investment and how guaranteed quick returns are a warning sign. She left saying she might start very small once she understood more, and would talk to her parents first. I've suggested she join next month's session on reading fund documents.

qa.q: What did Disha's uncle lose savings in?
qa.a: He lost savings in a scheme promising fixed high returns.

qa.q: Why was Disha scared to invest at all?
qa.a: Seeing her uncle lose money made her associate any investing with that loss, so fear held her back.

qa.q: How did Abhinav support Disha without pushing her?
qa.a: Abhinav asked what she already knew, explained that quick guaranteed returns are a warning sign, and suggested more learning rather than recommending a product.

qa.q: If you were Disha's parents, what might you want from this conversation?
qa.a: They might want her to feel safe discussing money with them and not rush into anything, which she said she would do.

grounding: Shows an adult advisor noting a student moving from fear toward understanding risk and spotting get-rich-quick schemes.

passage:
Thursday, 10 pm
Vijay bhaiya added me to a group today called 'Double Money Club'. Screenshots of people's 'profits', lots of rocket emojis, a man promising returns in thirty days if we join now. For a second I felt the pull, like everyone else is getting rich and I'm the slow one. Then I remembered Mamma's line: if someone is in a hurry for your money, walk away. I left the group. Bhaiya sent an angry face: 'Preeti, you'll regret it.' Fine. Instead I reread my notes from last month, when Mamma and I met an investment officer at our bank who explained things without selling me anything. Spreading money across different things so one bad fall doesn't wipe me out. Small amounts, regularly, growing slowly over years. Boring. I like boring now. Still need to read more before I decide anything.

qa.q: What was the group Vijay added Preeti to called?
qa.a: 'Double Money Club'.

qa.q: What pull did Preeti feel on seeing the group?
qa.a: A moment of fear of missing out, as if everyone else was getting rich while Preeti was the slow one.

qa.q: Which signs in the group did Preeti rightly treat as red flags?
qa.a: Promised returns in thirty days, pressure to join now and screenshots of 'profits' are signs of a get-rich-quick scheme.

qa.q: How might Vijay bhaiya feel about Preeti leaving the group?
qa.a: Annoyed, as his angry face shows, perhaps because he believes in it or felt his offer was turned down.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young adult walking away from a get-rich-quick group and choosing slow, diversified understanding instead.

passage:

qa.a: Since his internship, in very small amounts.

qa.q: What does Afreen's 'losing money would make me sick' reveal about her?

qa.q: Why is Zubin's suggestion to speak to a proper adviser wise?
qa.a: How much risk feels right is personal, and a qualified adviser can match choices to it better than a friend's or an uncle's tips.

passage: At the chai stall in Sehore, Lalit was selling a miracle. "Double in ninety days," he said, showing Akash a phone full of screenshots. "My cousin put in ten thousand in May. Got twenty by August." Akash had saved nineteen thousand from his tuition job, the most money he had ever had. His heart beat faster. Then he thought of his mother's gold that had vanished into a chit scheme when he was twelve, and how she had cried in the kitchen. "Who runs it?" he asked. Lalit shrugged. "Some company. Online." "Where's their office?" Another shrug. That evening Akash went to the post office and asked the clerk, who had known his family for years. She showed him leaflets for small, regular government savings schemes and said, "Nothing honest doubles in ninety days, beta. Talk to a registered adviser before you invest anything." Akash left his money in the bank.

qa.q: How much had Akash saved from his tuition job?
qa.a: Nineteen thousand.

qa.q: What made Akash's heart beat faster, and what cooled it?
qa.a: Akash felt excited imagining the money doubling, then wary and sad remembering his mother's gold lost in a chit scheme.

qa.q: Which questions helped Akash see the warning signs?
qa.a: Asking who runs it and where their office is; the vague answers showed the scheme couldn't be checked.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel if the scheme collapses?
qa.a: Lalit, who trusted his cousin's screenshots, would likely feel shocked and guilty, especially if he had drawn friends in.

grounding: In a small town, a young man resists a get-rich-quick scheme and asks a trusted clerk about safer, slower options.

passage: When Yuki got her first proper salary at a design agency in Osaka, she wanted to put every spare yen into one electric-car company her colleague was excited about. "It went up forty percent this year!" Jana, her flatmate from Prague, who was studying economics, winced. "And next year?" "Up again, obviously." Jana pulled a bowl of mixed rice crackers towards her. "If you only buy the wasabi ones and they're bad this year, you've got nothing. With a bit of everything, one bad flavour doesn't ruin the bowl." Yuki rolled her eyes but laughed. Together they looked up what "diversified" meant, and how small monthly amounts grow over many years because the growth itself starts growing. Yuki decided to book a session with an independent adviser before putting in anything. "Boring," she said. "Very boring," Jana agreed, crunching a wasabi one.

qa.q: How much had the car company gone up this year?
qa.a: Forty percent.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling about the car company?
qa.a: Yuki felt excited and confident, sure it would keep rising after one strong year.

qa.q: What did the rice-cracker comparison help Yuki understand?
qa.a: That spreading money across many things means one bad investment doesn't ruin everything, which is the idea of diversification.

qa.q: How does Jana see Yuki's plan?
qa.a: Jana sees it as risky, betting everything on one company after one good year, and feels worried on Yuki's behalf.

grounding: A young worker in Japan, helped by a flatmate, learns about diversification and compounding before investing.

passage: In his second week at the Pune office, Yogesh sat through the HR "money basics" session mostly for the free samosas. The speaker, Sarika, a certified financial planner, drew two lines on the whiteboard: one person investing a small amount every month from twenty-two, another investing more but starting at thirty-two. The early line ended higher. "Because the returns start earning returns," she said. "Time does the heavy lifting." Yogesh thought of the office chat group where a colleague posted daily "sure-shot" coin tips with rocket emojis. He raised his hand. "What about things that go up fast?" Sarika didn't mock him. "Ask three questions. Who regulates it? What if it falls by half? Could you explain it to your mother?" Yogesh had no answers for the coins. Afterwards he took her card, muted the tips group, and stuck a note on his monitor: ask before investing.

qa.q: What was Sarika's job?
qa.a: A certified financial planner.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he raised his hand?
qa.a: Yogesh was curious and a little tempted by the fast-rising coin tips, and unsure how they compared.

qa.q: Why are Sarika's three questions useful before any investment?
qa.a: They check whether something is regulated, whether a fall could be survived and whether it is understood, which exposes get-rich-quick schemes.

qa.q: How might Sarika see Yogesh's question?
qa.a: Sarika treats it as a fair question rather than a foolish one, and uses it to teach how to spot risky schemes.

grounding: At a workplace session, a young employee learns about compounding and how to question get-rich-quick tips.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,
I have to tell you something before you put money in that "trading group" your friend added you to.
Last year I joined one too. They promised to double money in a month. The screenshots of profits looked real. I put in my savings. For two weeks, it showed gains. Then the group admin disappeared, and so did my money.
I felt so stupid. I didn't tell anyone for months.
I've learnt since: if someone guarantees high returns quickly, it's a red flag. Real investing is slow and has risks. I now only use registered platforms, and I spoke to a registered financial adviser before starting anything.
Please talk to one before you do anything. I'll come with you if you want.
Sabina

qa.q: What did the trading group promise?
qa.a: To double money in a month.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling after losing the money?
qa.a: Sabina felt stupid and ashamed, keeping it secret for months.

qa.q: What does Sabina suggest Ujjwal do before investing?
qa.a: Talk to a registered financial adviser and use only registered platforms, not guaranteed-return groups.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ujjwal may feel surprised and thankful for Sabina's honesty and warning.

grounding: A young adult warns a friend about get-rich-quick investment schemes after losing money.

passage:
I'm Keerthana. You asked about the crypto group. Okay.
A cousin added me to a chat. Everyone posted screenshots of huge gains. "Get in now or miss out!" I felt left behind. So I put in my first salary.
The coin crashed in a week. I lost most of it.
I called my friend Lalit, who works in finance. He didn't laugh. He explained compounding: small amounts, invested steadily over years, can grow, but nothing is guaranteed. He said to spread money across different things, not bet everything on one. And to talk to a registered adviser about my own risk appetite.
Now I'm slow. Boring. But I sleep at night.

qa.q: What did Keerthana put into the coin?
qa.a: The first salary.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling seeing the screenshots of gains?
qa.a: Keerthana felt left behind and anxious to join in.

qa.q: What choice after the loss helped Keerthana?
qa.a: Calling Lalit, learning about compounding and diversification, and planning to see a registered adviser.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when Keerthana called?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt sympathetic and wanted to help, not judge.

grounding: A young adult tells how Keerthana lost money in a hyped scheme and learned about steady, diversified investing.

passage:
I'm Farhan, Sachin's flatmate. When Sachin got his first salary, I expected him to spend it on gadgets like I did.
Instead, he spent evenings reading about mutual funds and asking questions on the phone to a registered adviser his uncle knew. He wrote notes about risk and diversification.
He started a small monthly SIP. Just a small amount. When his friends showed off crypto gains, he shrugged.
Once the market fell and his fund went down. He looked worried for a day. Then he said, "The adviser said it goes up and down. I'm in for years."
I don't know if he'll get rich. But he seems calm about money in a way I'm not.

qa.q: What did Sachin start with a small amount?
qa.a: A small monthly SIP.

qa.q: What might Sachin have felt when the market fell?
qa.a: Sachin seemed worried for a day, then calm, remembering the adviser's advice.

qa.q: What did Sachin do that others starting out could learn from?
qa.a: He read, asked a registered adviser, understood risk and started small.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Sachin's approach to money?
qa.a: Farhan sees it as calm and steady, unlike his own spending.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young man starting small, informed investments and staying calm in a fall.

passage:
Monday: In the office canteen, Jagdish showed Ankita a group on his phone. "Double your money in thirty days. Crypto signals. Everyone's making lakhs."
Ankita, in her first job, felt the pull. Her salary felt small.
Wednesday: Her company held a free session by a registered financial adviser. He drew one line that grew slowly, then steeply: compounding. "Small amounts, over long time, spread across different things, beat big promises," he said. "If someone promises to double your money fast, walk away."
Friday: Jagdish's group had disappeared, along with the admin. Jagdish had lost what he'd put in. He sat with his head in his hands.
Ankita didn't say "I told you". She bought him chai. That evening she called her mother and made an appointment to talk to the adviser properly before deciding anything.

qa.q: What did the group on Jagdish's phone promise?
qa.a: "Double your money in thirty days."

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when Jagdish showed her the group?
qa.a: Ankita felt tempted, since her new salary felt small.

qa.q: Why was Ankita's plan to talk to the adviser before deciding a sound choice?
qa.a: It relies on a qualified person and time rather than a get-rich-quick promise, which is exactly the kind of offer the adviser warned about.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel when Ankita buys him chai instead of saying "I told you"?
qa.a: Jagdish probably feels ashamed but grateful for the kindness.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning about compounding and diversification and avoiding a get-rich-quick scheme.

passage:
Sarita, you asked why I'm so suspicious of schemes. When I was twenty-one and newly married, a lady in our colony started a "savings club". Monthly payments, and after a year you'd get back half as much again. All the women joined. I put in what I earned from tuitions.
For six months, it worked. People got paid, and more joined. Then one Monday her flat was locked. Gone. Forty families lost their money. I cried for days; I'd hidden it from my husband.
Later, a bank officer explained to our colony group how it worked: new people's money paid the old people, until there were no new people.
Since then my rule for myself is simple: if I don't understand where the money grows, I don't put it in. And I ask a proper adviser first. That's what your Nandini Mami knows.

qa.q: How many families lost their money?
qa.a: Forty families.

qa.q: How did young Nandini feel when the flat was locked?
qa.a: Young Nandini felt devastated and guilty, crying for days because she had hidden it from her husband.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nandini's understanding?
qa.a: The bank officer explaining that new members' money paid old members, so she saw why the scheme had to collapse.

qa.q: How might the lady's neighbours have felt after she vanished?
qa.a: The neighbours probably felt betrayed and ashamed, having trusted someone they knew.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recounting how a get-rich-quick savings club collapsed and why she seeks advice before investing.

passage:
Tanvir got his first salary in Dhaka in December, and it disappeared fast: rent, money home to his mother, a loan his brother had taken for college. What was left was tiny.
His colleague Elizabeth said she put a small amount into a monthly fund plan. "Even small helps, because of compounding. But I spread it; I don't put it all in one thing."
At the same time, a cousin kept sending him "hot stock tips" from a trading app group, promising fast profits.
Tanvir felt torn. The tips looked exciting. The small plan looked boring. He also felt guilty keeping anything for himself when his family needed it.
He asked Elizabeth how she'd chosen. She said she'd first spoken to a licensed adviser at her bank. Tanvir booked the same appointment for his lunch break, and muted the cousin's group until then.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir's first salary go?
qa.a: Rent, money home to his mother and his brother's college loan.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir feel torn?
qa.a: Tanvir felt tempted by the exciting tips, unsure about the boring plan, and guilty about keeping anything for himself when his family needed it.

qa.q: What choice did Tanvir make, and why is it a sensible one?
qa.a: He booked an appointment with a licensed adviser and muted the tips group, choosing qualified advice over quick-profit promises.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's mother feel about his first salary?
qa.a: His mother would probably feel proud and grateful for the money he sends home.

grounding: Shows a young adult with little money weighing small diversified investing against get-rich-quick tips and seeking advice.

passage: The message came from Nilesh's school friend on a Thursday night: a "trading group" where members "doubled their money in ninety days, guaranteed." Nilesh, three months into his first job in Pune, felt the pull. He had some savings sitting idle, and everyone at the office seemed to be talking about markets. At lunch he showed the screenshots to Sangeeta, a senior on his team. She scrolled, then put the phone down. "Guaranteed and doubled in the same sentence? That's the red flag. Real investments go up and down." She told him how she had started years ago: small, regular amounts spread across different kinds of funds, after sitting down with a registered adviser. "Boring. Slow. Mine still has bad months." Nilesh muted the group that evening. He booked a session at his bank's advisory desk for Saturday, and wrote his questions down first.

qa.q: What did the trading group claim?
qa.a: That members doubled their money in ninety days, guaranteed.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he first saw the message?
qa.a: He felt tempted and a little left out, with idle savings and colleagues all talking about markets.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that others could learn from?
qa.a: He showed the offer to someone experienced before acting, muted the group, and booked time with a qualified adviser, questions written down.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see the trading group?
qa.a: She sees it as a warning sign, because real investments go up and down, while the group promises a guaranteed double.

grounding: Shows a young earner turning away from a get-rich-quick scheme and learning that real investing is slow and spread out.
